meta.title: Dutch A1 Beginner
meta.subtitle: 500 words · both directions, as two cards per word
meta.desc: Both study directions in one deck: Dutch → English (see the Dutch, recall the meaning) and English → Dutch (see an English meaning, recall the Dutch). Each direction is a card of its own with its own schedule, so recognising a word and producing it are learnt separately. 500 words of Dutch for a beginner, aligned to A1 of the Common European Framework of Reference, whose global descriptor begins 'Can understand and use familiar everyday expressions and very basic phrases aimed at the satisfaction of needs of a concrete type' — a learner here is able to introduce themselves and others, to ask and answer questions about personal details such as where they live, people they know and things they have, and to interact in a simple way provided the other person talks slowly and clearly and is prepared to help. WHERE THESE WORDS COME FROM, since it matters: Dutch has examinations at these levels — the inburgeringsexamen, the Staatsexamen NT2 and the CNaVT — but no graded word list for them was found published, so this deck is not any examination's vocabulary and does not claim to be. It is assembled from two things that can be stated. 380 of the 500 come from a vocabulary written for the level's scope — greetings and politeness, introducing yourself, family, numbers, telling the time, days and months, food and drink, shopping and money, the home, the town and getting about, the body and feeling ill, the weather, colours, and the articles, pronouns, question words, prepositions and small words every sentence is built out of — and the other 120 are the commonest remaining words of everyday Dutch, taken from a frequency list built from film and television subtitles and counted by the WHOLE word, every form of a verb or an adjective added together. The cards are dealt by that frequency, so the words you meet most often come first. Every headword has its pronunciation beneath it in the International Phonetic Alphabet, Wiktionary's own. The 170 nouns are printed with their article — de or het — because nothing in a Dutch noun says which it takes, and they show their plural and diminutive; the 90 verbs show their past and past participle (eten, at, gegeten), and behind the All forms fold their present and past by person, imperative and participles. Real example sentences come with 500 of the 500 words, three apiece for 499 of them, with the word picked out in colour and a speaker beside the sentence and the headword. Sources. Level: the Common European Framework of Reference (Council of Europe), global scale. Meanings, gender, forms and pronunciation: English Wiktionary, via the kaikki.org extraction (CC BY-SA 4.0). Frequency: a word list built from OpenSubtitles (hermitdave/FrequencyWords, CC BY-SA 4.0). Example sentences: Tatoeba (tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR.
